# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# Critical Reading: Two-Year Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Halden Subset

**Bottom line:** This is the most informative document of the five. It answers the question every earlier paper left open, whether the gains last. It does so with stronger hours measurement and a mediation analysis registered before the outcomes were known. The core result is credible: a per-hour gain of about 8.5–10% that persists at 24 months, smaller than at nine months but well clear of zero.

There are four main problems:
- The two control offices that cut their own meetings contaminated the control group. That could explain part of the apparent fade, and the paper does not adjust for it.
- The mediation analysis is described as confirming the meetings hypothesis. It is a pre-specified test on the same offices that generated the hypothesis, not a replication.
- It is unclear how the log-in measure treats meeting time. That matters for interpreting the mediation result.
- A marketing agency's reversion is folded into "coverage obligations" when it does not fit that category.

## 1. The arithmetic checks out, with one figure that needs explaining

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Output per hour, timesheets | 0.966 / 0.88 = **+9.8%**. Correct. |
| Output per hour, system logs | 0.966 / 0.89 = **+8.5%**. Correct. |
| Halden continuers | 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866; 96.8 / 86.6 = **+11.8%**. Correct. |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 = 100. Correct. |
| Counter offices, 12% more staff | 1.12 × 0.83 (hours) × 1.067 (per-hour gain) ≈ 0.99 of baseline output. **Consistent.** |
| Counter offices, cost +9% | 12% more staff on unchanged pay raises the **labour** cost per contact by about 12%. The 9% figure holds only if labour is roughly 75% of total cost, or the extra staff cost less. **This needs explaining.** |

**The Summary compares different measures.** It says the gain "fell from 12.5% to 8.5%", but 12.5% was measured on timesheets and 8.5% on system logs. The like-for-like decline is 12.5% → 9.8%, about a fifth, not a third. The body of the paper gets this right; the Summary should too.

## 2. What the paper does well

- **It directly answers the questions left open.** It tests persistence, tests the meetings hypothesis under a registered plan, and checks whether timesheets understated hours.
- **Hours are measured more strictly.** Log-in data capture unclaimed work and, as suspected, show slightly more hours than timesheets.
- **The mediation plan was registered at month 11**, before the 24-month outcomes existed.
- **The counter-office evidence is improved.** Waiting times are now compared with control offices (7.3 vs 4.0 minutes), fixing the treated-only comparison flagged in the nine-month report. The county's decision to end the arm is real-world confirmation of the result for coverage-bound work.
- **Halden's data are described honestly.** The continuers are called "survivors twice over" and their figures an upper bound, not an estimate.
- **The rebuttals are precise.** The finding that all four long-run studies in the meta-analysis were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours confirms the earlier concern about the meta-analysis's no-decay claim.

## 3. The control offices' meeting audit contaminates the comparison

In month 15, two of the seven **control** offices cut their recurring meetings, and their output per hour rose 4.1%. The paper presents this only as a hint that the gain might be achievable without cutting hours. But it also affects the main estimate:

- **The control group improved.** If those two offices are similar in size to the others, control output per hour rose by roughly 1.2 points on average. That shrinks the treated-versus-control gap at 24 months by about the same amount.
- **The "fade" may be partly a control effect.** The like-for-like decline is 2.7 points (12.5 → 9.8). Perhaps 1 point of that comes from control offices improving, not from treated offices declining.
- **The cause may be the trial itself.** The nine-month report publicised the meetings finding. Control staff may have acted on it.

The authors should report a sensitivity analysis that excludes those two offices, or that ends before month 15. Without one, the 24-month estimate is probably slightly *understated*, and the extent of fading is overstated.

## 4. The mediation analysis is weaker than "confirms" suggests

- **It is the same sample, not a replication.** The hypothesis came from these seven treated offices, and the registered test uses the same offices. Registering before the outcomes guards against fitting the analysis to the results. It does not answer Varga and Holm's concern about whether the finding would replicate elsewhere.
- **The effective sample is still 14 offices.** "A larger sample of office-months" adds repeated measures, but monthly observations within an office are not independent. Intervals such as 47% (28 to 66) depend on handling clustering properly with so few clusters. The method is not stated.
- **The meetings mediator is not randomised.** Managers who cut more meetings may also manage better in other ways. The Limitations section acknowledges this, but "confirms" in the Summary overstates what mediation analysis can show.
- **The baseline meeting data are unexplained.** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six. This report gives baseline figures of 7.4 and 7.2 hours. If these were extracted retrospectively from calendars, that is fine, but the paper should say so.
- **The hours measure may not include meetings.** System logs record "time staff are working on cases." If meetings are not logged, cutting meetings does not reduce the denominator. In that case, the meetings pathway can work only indirectly, for example through fewer interruptions to case work. That is a different and less obvious mechanism than "removing low-value hours." If meetings *are* logged, the measure is not what its description says. Either way the paper needs to state which.

Even with these reservations, the result substantially weakens the claim that meetings are "a post hoc story." The paper also correctly notes that it cannot say whether reorganising work without cutting hours would capture most of the gain.

## 5. Several outcomes are missing

- **Backlogs and statutory deadlines.** The nine-month report named backlog growth as the key risk to watch. Output per employee has drifted from −2.1% to −3.4% with unchanged inflow, so backlogs are probably growing. The 24-month report does not mention deadlines.
- **Cost in case-processing offices.** Cost per contact is estimated for the counter offices, but not for case-processing. With pay unchanged and output per FTE at −3.4%, cost per case is up about 3.5%, plus any overtime paid.
- **Whether the change is statistically real.** The 9- and 24-month intervals overlap heavily (6.9 to 18.4 vs 4.6 to 15.2). "Consistent with some fading" is fair, but the decline is not statistically established.
- **Uncertainty for wellbeing.** Sick days (−27%) and resignations are still reported without confidence intervals.

## 6. The Halden follow-up has three problems

- **Missing responses.** Only 14 of the 23 organisations with records responded. The 9 non-responders could include further reversions.
- **The reversion count is ambiguous.** The original Halden paper listed five reversions at month six, three in retail and hospitality. It is unclear whether the hospitality group and retail chain here are among those earlier reversions or are new ones. If they are earlier ones, describing them as reversions found at 24 months is misleading.
- **A discretionary organisation reverted.** The marketing agency cited client deadlines, which is discretionary work under the meta-analysis's coding. The Summary's phrase "client-facing or coverage obligations" stretches the category to fit it. This is a modest but real piece of evidence that discretionary work does not always sustain reduced hours.

Note also that a Halden author co-authors this report. The treatment of the Halden data is candid, so this is a point of context, not a criticism.

## 7. How it answers the earlier claims

| Earlier claim | Status after this report |
|---|---|
| Halden: model works in every sector, +23.4% | **Rejected.** The counter arm was ended on cost and service grounds, and reversions cluster in coverage-bound settings. |
| Varga and Holm: gains are "entirely artifact" | **Rejected.** About 8.5% remains under the standards they recommended. The novelty account is also weakened: the earlier energy extrapolation implied the gain would vanish by about month 9–10, but at 24 months it still exceeds 8%. |
| Varga and Holm: the meetings hypothesis is post hoc | **Weakened.** It survives a registered test, but in the same sample. |
| Meta-analysis: no decay, so novelty can be set aside | **Rejected as argued.** The long-run studies were all weak designs. The real evidence shows modest fading, about a fifth, which may be partly a control-group effect. |
| Meta-analysis: roughly 8–10% gain in better studies | **Corroborated.** |

## 8. Synthesis across all five documents

**What the evidence now supports:**
1. **Discretionary work.** Reduced hours produce a durable per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% over two years. That offsets most, but not all, of the lost hours: output per employee is down about 3%, so cost per unit of output rises slightly.
2. **Coverage-bound work.** Output and service fall. Restoring service requires roughly 12% more staff, so the scheme does not pay for itself.
3. **Mechanism.** A substantial part of the gain is linked to cutting low-value time such as recurring meetings. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less.
4. **Measurement.** Headline figures above 20% come mainly from using scheduled rather than actual hours, manager ratings and self-selected samples.

**What remains open:**
- Whether reorganising work *without* cutting hours captures most of the gain. No trial has tested this, and the control offices' meeting audit is suggestive only.
- Generalisability beyond one public employer with seven offices per arm.
- Effects beyond 24 months.
- Backlog and deadline performance in the case-processing offices.
